items.topic: Initiative card — progress bar style and status distribution visualization
items.context: The card needs to show both overall progress (completed/total) and per-status item distribution. Two visual elements compete for space: a progress bar and status dots/chips. The choice affects information density and scannability. The existing RollupStatus provides total, completed, in_progress, failed, and pending counts.

options.label: Stacked progress bar (segmented by status) + numeric breakdown below
options.rationale: Single bar shows both progress AND distribution. Segments colored by status (green=completed, cyan=in_progress, red=failed, gray=pending). Numeric counts shown as compact text row below the bar (e.g., '3 ready · 2 running · 1 failed'). Most space-efficient. Recommended because it encodes two dimensions of information in one visual element while keeping the card compact.

options.label: Simple progress bar (completed only) + separate colored dot row
options.rationale: Progress bar shows only completed/total (simple green fill). Separate row of colored dots shows per-status counts. Two distinct visual elements — easier to read but takes more vertical space.

options.label: Donut/ring chart for status distribution
options.rationale: Compact circular visualization showing all statuses as segments. Looks polished but harder to compare across cards and may be overkill for a text-heavy dashboard.

items.topic: Priority badge visual treatment on initiative cards
items.context: Each initiative card shows a priority (1-10). The badge needs to communicate urgency at a glance without dominating the card. Priority 1 is highest/most urgent, 10 is lowest.

options.label: Colored number badge with gradient (red=1-3, amber=4-6, green=7-10)
options.rationale: Color encodes urgency: hot colors for high priority, cool for low. Small pill with just the number. Recommended because it provides instant visual scanning across the card grid — you can spot high-priority initiatives without reading text.

options.label: Monochrome number badge with varying opacity/weight
options.rationale: Subtle — priority 1 gets bold/full opacity, priority 10 gets light/faded. Less visual noise but harder to scan quickly across many cards.

options.label: Named priority tiers instead of numbers (Critical, High, Medium, Low)
options.rationale: More semantic but takes more horizontal space and adds a mapping layer (which numbers map to which tier?).

items.topic: Needs Attention feed — refresh interval and notification behavior
items.context: The Needs Attention feed aggregates data from 4 sources via react-query. The refresh interval affects how quickly new issues surface. Too frequent wastes resources; too slow means stale data. Related: the agents dropdown already refreshes every 5 seconds.

options.label: 30-second refetch for all dashboard data, no toast notifications
options.rationale: Balanced refresh rate. Dashboard is a pull model — users check it when they want to. No interruptions. Recommended because the dashboard is a status board, not an alerting system. Users visit it intentionally.

options.label: 60-second refetch with subtle badge count on Dashboard tab when new items appear
options.rationale: Slower refresh but adds a notification dot on the Dashboard tab (like unread messages) when new attention items appear since last visit. More discoverable but adds state tracking complexity.

options.label: Manual refresh only (button in feed header)
options.rationale: Simplest implementation. User clicks refresh when they want fresh data. May feel stale for users who leave the dashboard open.

items.context: This research item produces specifications. The implementation work needs to be split into execute items. The question is how to decompose — one large item vs. multiple focused items. The components have some data dependencies (e.g., initiative cards need priority field to exist) but are otherwise independent UI work.

options.label: Three execute items: (1) Initiative schema + settings dialog, (2) Dashboard page, (3) Tab/navigation changes
options.rationale: Schema changes in item 1 unblock card sorting in item 2. Settings dialog is small and pairs naturally with schema work. Navigation changes are a separate concern. Recommended because it creates a clear dependency chain: 1→2→3, each independently testable.

options.label: Two execute items: (1) Dashboard page + initiative schema, (2) Settings relocation + nav changes
options.rationale: Fewer items, bigger scope each. Dashboard needs schema changes anyway so they bundle naturally. Settings + nav are the 'remove old, add new' pair.

options.label: Single execute item: implement everything at once
options.rationale: Simplest tracking. Everything ships together so no partial states. But large scope makes review harder and increases risk of conflicts.

items.text: The SettingsPage is 6 card sections (Theme, Execution Defaults, Workshop, Agent Behavior, UI Preferences, Save footer) — confirmed at ~558 lines with per-section reset buttons, dirty checking, navigation blocker, and conditional field visibility. The dialog adaptation will need to handle the internal scroll context carefully since the page was designed for full-viewport height.

The current BacklogStatus type includes 'researching' and 'queued' statuses not mentioned in the original rollup. The stats bar should use the full status set: backlog, researching, ready, queued, in_progress, completed, failed, archived. The 'Active Items' stat should count everything except completed and archived. Consider whether 'researching' and 'queued' deserve their own stats or fold into the existing categories.
